name: Tilt-shift
summary: Lens or camera movements that keep vertical lines parallel and move the plane of focus; a building stands upright and sharp.
how: Keep the back of the camera vertical and shift the lens up by 10 to 20 mm, so that vertical lines stay parallel.
Tilt the lens by 2° to 8° to turn the plane of focus along the ground for depth at a small stop.
Close the lens to f/11 to f/22 for full depth of field.
In an editor, use a narrow band of focus and a strong blur outside it to fake a miniature.

origin.note: Theodor Scheimpflug patents the rule for tilted lens and plane of focus.

adoptions.via: Paul Strand and Alfred Stieglitz use large view cameras for sharp, unretouched prints.
Group f/64 use large-format view cameras with small stops and sharp focus from front to back.
Julius Shulman photographs Case Study House No. 22 on a large-format camera with upright lines.
Nikon sells the PC-Nikkor 35mm f/3.5, the first shift lens for a 35mm camera.
Stephen Shore and Joel Sternfeld use 8 x 10 in view cameras with movements for large colour prints.
Food photographers tilt the plane of focus so that one bite is sharp and the rest falls away.
Interior photographers for Nordic magazines and blogs use shift lenses to keep walls vertical.
Photoshop CS6 adds the Tilt-Shift blur filter, and the miniature look spreads on the web.
Octopath Traveler blurs the top and bottom of each frame so the world reads as a miniature.
